stem: A 68-year-old woman with Parkinson's disease (on levodopa/carbidopa 100/25mg five times daily, pramipexole 0.7mg TDS, and procyclidine 5mg TDS) is admitted to hospital after a fall. The orthopaedic team is concerned she is 'confused and seeing things'. On assessment, she describes vivid visual hallucinations of children in the room, which she initially believed were real but now doubts. She is alert, oriented, and has no fever or autonomic instability. Observations are normal. She has been on the same medications for 3 years without change. No recent infection or electrolyte disturbance. What is the MOST appropriate first step?
options: Add quetiapine 12.5mg nocte for management of visual hallucinations

Reduce and discontinue PROCYCLIDINE (anticholinergic) FIRST — anticholinergics are the most common cause of confusion/hallucinations in Parkinson's, and this patient does not need an anticholinergic if she has not had extrapyramidal side effects
Start rivastigmine 1.5mg BD for possible Lewy body dementia
Request CT head to rule out a space-occupying lesion
distractors_rationale: Quetiapine should NOT be the first step. The first step in Parkinson's disease psychosis (PDP) is ALWAYS to review and reduce medications (anticholinergics first, then dopamine agonists, then COMT-I, then MAO-B-I, then levodopa LAST). Only after medication optimisation has failed should an antipsychotic be considered.

CORRECT. The first step in PDP management is a SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND REDUCTION of dopaminergic/anticholinergic medications IN ORDER: (1) ANTICHOLINERGICS — FIRST (procyclidine, trihexyphenidyl, benzatropine). These drugs block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and can cause CONFUSION, HALLUCINATIONS, and COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT, especially in older patients. They should be DISCONTINUED if there is no history of significant EPS. In this patient, procyclidine 5mg TDS is a HIGH dose for a 68-year-old with Parkinson's and should be REDUCED/DISCONTINUED. (2) AMANTADINE — second (can cause confusion and psychosis). (3) DOPAMINE AGONISTS — third (pramipexole — highest risk of psychosis among PD meds). (4) COMT INHIBITORS — fourth (entacapone). (5) MAO-B INHIBITORS — fifth (selegiline, rasagiline). (6) LEVODOPA — LAST (lowest psychosis risk, best motor efficacy). The question states: 'no recent infection or electrolyte disturbance' and 'on the same meds for 3 years' — so the cause may be the medications themselves. WHY HAS THIS STARTED NOW? Possibly because of the STRESS of the fall/hospitalisation, or an age-related decline in cholinergic function unmasking the anticholinergic burden.

Rivastigmine is indicated for MILD-MODERATE DEMENTIA with LEWY BODIES (DLB) and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD). This patient has no evidence of cognitive impairment (she is alert, oriented, full MMSE not mentioned). Cognitive assessment should be done before starting a ChEI. The anti-muscarinic effect of anticholinergic medications can cause iatrogenic cognitive impairment that mimics DLB.
CT head may be indicated if there are focal neurological signs. The absence of such signs means it is not the MOST appropriate first step. The first step is medication review.
Benzodiazepines are NOT recommended for PDP — they can cause paradoxical disinhibition, falls, and dependence. They may be useful short-term for severe agitation after all other options have failed.
teaching_point: Anticholinergic burden in the elderly — HIGH-YIELD: (1) Anticholinergic drugs block muscarinic receptors (M1 subtype centrally responsible for cognitive function). This can cause: CONFUSION, DELIRIUM, HALLUCINATIONS (especially visual), MEMORY IMPAIRMENT, AGITATION. Peripheral anticolinergic effects: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, dry skin. (2) ANTICHOLINERGICS IN PARKINSON'S: Procyclidine, trihexyphenidyl, benzatropine — used to treat drug-induced parkinsonism (EPS from antipsychotics) and Parkinson's disease. They are HIGHLY ANTICHOLINERGIC and should be AVOIDED in elderly patients with cognitive concerns. (3) THE 'ANTICHOLINERGIC LOAD' — the cumulative effect of multiple drugs with anticholinergic activity. Many drugs have weak anticholinergic properties: some SSRIs (paroxetine — moderate), antihistamines, oxybutynin (for urinary incontinence), tricyclics (amitriptyline — highly anticholinergic). ALWAYS assess anticholinergic burden in elderly patients with confusion! (4) The 'start low, go slow' rule applies to all psychotropics in the elderly. (5) The Maudsley Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic drugs should be avoided in elderly patients, in those with cognitive impairment, and in those on multiple medications.' (6) Anticholinergics should be the FIRST medications withdrawn in patients with PDP.
source: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; NICE NG71: Parkinson's disease; BNF (anticholinergic effects)

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a history of moderate depression presents with her first manic episode. She has been agitated, expansive, not sleeping, and has grandiose delusions (saying she 'will cure world hunger'). She is treated with olanzapine 15mg daily, which settles the episode over 4 weeks. She is now euthymic. She is NOT on a mood stabiliser. She has had ONE manic episode and NO depressive episodes (the depressive episode was earlier but does not meet the duration or severity for major depression). She asks about LONG-TERM treatment. According to NICE CG185, what is the MOST appropriate recommendation?
options: Offer LONG-TERM maintenance treatment (lithium first-line) because she has had one manic episode — the recurrence risk is high
Offer no long-term treatment — a single manic episode does not require maintenance therapy; monitor and start treatment if another episode occurs
Offer lithium OR valproate for maintenance
Offer a long-acting injectable antipsychotic for maintenance
distractors_rationale: NICE CG185 states: 'Offer maintenance treatment to people who have had TWO or more episodes of bipolar disorder (mania, depression, or mixed episodes) OR ONE episode AND a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder.' This patient has ONE manic episode with NO family history and only one depressive episode that did not meet the criteria for major depression. Therefore, maintenance treatment is NOT indicated.

CORRECT. NICE CG185 does NOT recommend immediate maintenance treatment after a SINGLE MANIC EPISODE unless there are ADDITIONAL RISK FACTORS (e.g., family history, residual symptoms, severe episode with risk, substance misuse). The evidence: the recurrence rate after a first manic episode is approximately 50-60% within 2-5 years. This is a significant risk BUT maintenance treatment carries its own burden (side effects, monitoring, teratogenicity). The NICE recommendation is to discuss with the patient: (1) The RISK of recurrence (50-60% within 2-5 years); (2) The BENEFITS of treatment (reducing relapse risk by ~40-50%); (3) The SIDE EFFECTS of long-term treatment (lithium: renal, thyroid; antipsychotics: metabolic, EPS; valproate: teratogenicity, metabolic). If the patient chooses NOT to start maintenance: (1) Provide a RELAPSE PREVENTION PLAN (early warning signs, crisis plan); (2) Continue olanzapine for 3-6 months post-remission (NICE: 'Continue the antipsychotic for at least 3-6 months after resolution of a manic episode, then at the lowest effective dose); (3) PSYCHOEDUCATION (sleep hygiene, stress management, substance avoidance); (4) MONITOR for early signs of recurrence. If the patient chooses maintenance: lithium is first-line.

Valproate is not first-line for maintenance (even though it is commonly used). Lithium is the first-line maintenance treatment. Valproate is an alternative if lithium is not tolerated or is ineffective.
Quetiapine is effective for bipolar depression and for maintenance but is not first-line for maintenance in bipolar I. Lithium is first-line.
LAI is not appropriate without evidence of adherence problems and after only one episode.
teaching_point: When to start maintenance treatment in bipolar disorder (NICE CG185): (1) Offer maintenance to patients with TWO OR MORE episodes (mania, depression, or mixed) OR ONE episode + a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder. (2) If there is only ONE episode: discuss the risks vs benefits but do NOT automatically recommend maintenance. (3) FIRST-LINE MAINTENANCE: LITHIUM — strongest evidence for preventing both manic and depressive episodes. Also reduces suicide risk by ~60%. (4) Second-line options: valproate (if lithium not tolerated/ineffective — BUT restricted in women of childbearing potential). Olanzapine (metabolic side effects concern). Quetiapine (sedation, metabolic). Lamotrigine (stronger for depression than mania). (5) Duration: 'Continue maintenance treatment for at least 2 years after a manic episode, and for longer if there are risk factors for relapse (frequent episodes, severe episodes, poor insight, substance misuse).' (6) Discontinuation: if decided, taper GRADUALLY over at least 4-8 weeks (abrupt cessation can trigger early relapse — especially with lithium). (7) FIRST-EPISODE MANIA WITHOUT MOOD STABILISER: continue the antipsychotic (used for the acute episode) for 3-6 months after remission, then taper. Consider maintenance only if there are additional risk factors.
source: NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder; Goodwin GM & Malhi GS (2007) BAP Guidelines

stem:
Theme: Delirium — Identification and Management

For each scenario, select the CORRECT diagnosis/management step:

A. Delirium — hyperactive subtype
B. Delirium — hypoactive subtype
C. Delirium — mixed subtype
D. Dementia — Alzheimer's type
E. Dementia — Lewy body type
F. Dementia — vascular type
G. Depression
H. Psychosis
I. 4AT screening score >4
J. CAM-ICU positive
K. Treat the underlying cause
L. Haloperidol 0.5-1mg PO for severe distress
M. Haloperidol 5-10mg IM PRN
N. Environmental measures first
options: A 72-year-old man on day 3 post-hip replacement who is LETHARGIC, has reduced motor activity, is slow to respond to questions, and is mildly confused. He has no agitation. His daughter says he has 'not been himself'. The nurse thinks he has depression. What is the most likely diagnosis?

An 82-year-old woman in a care home with moderate Alzheimer's disease (MMSE 14) develops ACUTE ONSET of agitation, shouting, trying to climb out of bed, and pulling at her clothes over 48 hours. Temp 37.8°C. Urine dip shows leucocytes and nitrites. What is the most appropriate IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT?

A 28-year-old man with alcohol dependence (recent binge) is found in the street, disoriented, with visual hallucinations (insects crawling on him), tachycardia (130 bpm), hypertension (180/100), and hyperthermia (38.5°C). What is the diagnosis?
distractors_rationale: DELIRIUM — HYPACTIVE SUBTYPE (B). Hypoactive delirium is the MOST COMMON but MOST FREQUENTLY MISSED subtype (especially in the elderly). Presentation: LETHARGY, REDUCED MOTOR ACTIVITY, SLOWNESS, QUIET CONFUSION, WITHDRAWAL, DAYTIME SLEEPINESS, HYPNODELIRIUM (the patient appears sleepy/withdrawn). It is OFTEN MISDIAGNOSED AS DEPRESSION (the key difference: the ACUTE ONSET, FLUCTUATING COURSE, and cognitive impairment point to delirium, not depression). Risk factors: older age, dementia, polypharmacy, sensory impairment, severe illness. ASSESSMENT: The 4AT is the recommended screening tool for delirium (NICE CG103): (1) Alertness (0-2); (2) AMT4 (Abbreviated Mental Test — 0-4); (3) Attention (Months Backwards — 0-1); (4) Acute change or fluctuating course (0-4). Score >4 = possible delirium. the 4AT score >4 (I) would apply here. The KEY: Hypoactive delirium is just as serious as hyperactive delirium (same mortality risk) but is often missed. The 'DEPRESSION MIMICKY': 'He's just a bit down after the operation' vs 'He has acute confusion due to the stress of surgery + anaesthetic + opioids + dehydration + sleep deprivation.'

ENVIRONMENTAL MEASURES FIRST (N) — THEN treat the underlying cause (K) — AND low-dose haloperidol if severely distressed (L). This patient has DELIRIUM SUPERIMPOSED ON DEMENTIA (DSD). The management: (1) TREAT THE CAUSE — in this case, the UTI (start antibiotics). (2) ENVIRONMENTAL MEASURES: Reassure and reorient (use clocks, calendars, family photos), low lighting at night, uninterrupted sleep, sensory aids (glasses, hearing aids), familiar staff, family presence, avoid room changes. These non-pharmacological measures should be tried FIRST for mild-moderate agitation. (3) If she is SEVERELY AGITATED (shouting, climbing out of bed, pulling at clothes — which IS described): consider LOW-DOSE haloperidol 0.5-1mg (L) for the shortest duration possible (max 3-5 days). (4) AVOID: benzos (can worsen confusion), high-dose antipsychotics (falls, QTc risk, EPS). The response to the finding of a UTI should be antibiotics (not antipsychotics). The right answer: START ANTIBIOTICS AND ENVIRONMENTAL MEASURES FIRST. Only use haloperidol if severe distress persists despite these measures.

DELIRIUM TREMENS (DTs) — a SEVERE ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL PRESENTATION (C is hyperactive, but DTs is specifically the withdrawal delirium). (1) DIAGNOSIS: DELIRIUM TREMENS — acute confusion + visual hallucinations (insects, animals, 'formication') + autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia) + tremor. Onset: 48-96 hours after last drink. Mortality: ~5% untreated. (2) MANAGEMENT: MEDICAL EMERGENCY. (a) HIGH-DOSE BENZODIAZEPINES (diazepam 10-20mg IV/lorazepam 2-4mg IV) — titrate to sedation; (b) IV THIAMINE (Pabrinex); (c) SUPPORTIVE: IV fluids, cooling, electrolyte correction, monitoring (RR, HR, BP, Temp, SpO2); (d) HDU/ICU admission if severe or not responding; (e) Avoid antipsychotics (can lower seizure threshold, worsen DTs). Haloperidol M (5-10mg IM) is sometimes used for severe agitation in DTs but is NOT first-line (benzodiazepines are the first-line). The question asks for 'diagnosis' — it is DTs. The management is HIGH-DOSE BZD + IV THIAMINE.
teaching_point: Delirium subtypes and management (NICE CG103): (1) HYPERACTIVE: agitated, disoriented, hyper-alert, restless — EASIEST to recognise (often noticed by nursing staff). (2) HYPACTIVE: lethargic, withdrawn, sleepy, reduced motor activity — OFTEN MISSED (diagnosed as depression). (3) MIXED: features of BOTH — most common pattern. ALL subtypes have: (a) ACUTE ONSET; (b) FLUCTUATING COURSE; (c) REDUCED ATTENTION; (d) DISORGANISED THINKING. RISK FACTORS: age ≥65, cognitive impairment/dementia, severe illness, polypharmacy, sensory impairment, dehydration, constipation, surgery/anaesthesia, multiple medical problems. PREVENTION: multi-component intervention (NICE: orienting communication, therapeutic activities, mobilisation, nutrition, sleep hygiene, medication review — the 'HELP' programme: Hospital Elder Life Program). MANAGEMENT ABCS: (1) ALWAYS treat the UNDERLYING CAUSE (most common: infection, electrolyte, medication, hypoxia, constipation, pain, retention). (2) BEHAVIOURAL: environmental + family presence. (3) CHEMICAL: low-dose haloperidol 0.5-1mg PO — only if severe distress/risk. (4) STOP: benzodiazepines (except withdrawal), high doses, long-term antipsychotics. SCREENING: 4AT (alertness, AMT4, attention, acute change).
source: NICE CG103: Delirium; 4AT screening tool (MacLullich et al., 2011); BNF
